\begin{frame}{Your Turn: Find the Truth Value}

\prob{1}{1}{Let $p$ represent a false statement and $q$ represent a true statement. Find the truth value of each compound statement.}{$\sim p$} 

\prob{2}{2}{Let $p$ represent a false statement and $q$ represent a true statement. Find the truth value of each compound statement.}{$p \vee \sim q$} 

\prob{3}{3}{Let $p$ represent a false statement and $q$ represent a true statement. Find the truth value of each compound statement.}{$\sim (p \vee \sim q)$} 
\end{frame}

\begin{frame}{Your Turn: Find the Truth Value}

\prob{1}{1}{Let $p$ represent a true statement, and $q$ and $r$  represent false statements. Find the truth value of each compound statement.}{$(q \vee \sim r) \wedge p$} 

\prob{2}{2}{Let $p$ represent a true statement, and $q$ and $r$  represent false statements. Find the truth value of each compound statement.}{$(\sim p \wedge q) \vee \sim r$} 
\end{frame}

\begin{frame}{Your Turn: Find the Truth Value}

\prob{1}{1}{Let $p$ be the statement``$2>7$'', $q$ be statement ``$8 \leq 6$,'' and $r$ be the statement ``$19 \leq 19$.'' Find the truth value of each compound statement.}{$\sim p \vee \sim r$}

\prob{2}{2}{Let $p$ be the statement``$2>7$'', $q$ be statement ``$8 \leq 6$,'' and $r$ be the statement ``$19 \leq 19$.'' Find the truth value of each compound statement.}{$(p \wedge q) \vee r$}

\prob{3}{3}{Let $p$ be the statement``$2>7$'', $q$ be statement ``$8 \leq 6$,'' and $r$ be the statement ``$19 \leq 19$.'' Find the truth value of each compound statement.}{$(\sim r \wedge q) \vee \sim p$}
\end{frame}

\begin{frame}{Truth Tables: Conditional, i.e., ``if$\dots$then''}

\ex{1}{}{Construct a truth table for the statement ``If you give me $\$50$ then I will give you a ticket''.}

\vspace{-.75cm}
\begin{columns}


\column{11cm}
\begin{itemize}
\item []$p:$ You gave me $\$50$.
\item []$q$: I gave you a ticket.
\item []\only<2->{%
\begin{tabular}{cc|cc}
 & \multicolumn{1}{c}{} &  & \tabularnewline
\textbf{$p$} & \textbf{$q$} & \textbf{$p\rightarrow q$} & \tabularnewline
\cline{1-3}
\uT{3}{} & \uT{3}{} & \uT{4}{} & \tabularnewline
\uT{3}{} & \uF{3}{} & \uF{5}{} & \tabularnewline
\uF{3}{} & \uT{3}{} & \uT{6}{} & \uncover<7->{Because $p\rightarrow q$ is not false}\tabularnewline
\uF{3}{} & \uF{3}{} & \uT{8}{} & \uncover<9->{Because $p\rightarrow q$ is not false}\tabularnewline
\end{tabular}}
\end{itemize}
\end{columns}
\end{frame}

\begin{frame}{Problems}

\prob{1}{1}{Translate the compound statement into symbolic form and the construct the truth table for the expression.}{If it is raining then the streets are wet.}

\prob{2}{2}{Translate the compound statement into symbolic form and the construct the truth table for the expression.}{The water supply is rationned if it does not rain.}\prob{3}{3}{Translate the compound statement into symbolic form and the construct the truth table for the expression.}{All triangles are polygons.}\prob{4}{4}{Translate the compound statement into symbolic form and the construct the truth table for the expression.}{No hexagon is a triangle.}\prob{5}{5}{Translate the compound statement into symbolic form and the construct the truth table for the expression.}{Being a triangle is sufficient for not being a square.}\prob{6}{6}{Translate the compound statement into symbolic form and the construct the truth table for the expression.}{Not being a triangle is necessary for being a square.}

\prob{7}{7}{Translate the compound statement into symbolic form and the construct the truth table for the expression.}{If he does not go to jail, then he is innocent or has an alibi.}\prob{8}{8}{Translate the compound statement into symbolic form and the construct the truth table for the expression.}{If proposition A passes and Proposition B does not, jobs are lost or taxes will be raised.}
\end{frame}

\begin{frame}{Equivalent Statements}

\ex{1}{}{\center
\begin{enumerate}
\item The streets are wet, or it is not raining. \uncover<3->{$p\vee\sim q$}
\item If it is raining, then the streets are wet. \uncover<4->{$p\rightarrow q$} 
\end{enumerate}
}
\begin{columns}


\column{5cm}
\begin{itemize}
\item []<2->$p$: The streets are wet
\item []<2->$q:$ it is raining
\end{itemize}

\column{6cm}
\begin{itemize}
\item []\only<5->{%
\begin{tabular}{cc|c|c}
 & \multicolumn{1}{c}{} & \multicolumn{1}{c}{\circled{1}} & \circled{2}\tabularnewline
\textbf{$p$} & \textbf{$q$} & $p\vee\sim q$ & \textbf{$q\rightarrow p$}\tabularnewline
\hline 
\uT{6}{} & \uT{6}{} & \uT{7}{} & \uT{9}{}\tabularnewline
\uT{6}{} & \uF{6}{} & \uT{7}{} & \uT{10}{}\tabularnewline
\uF{6}{} & \uT{6}{} & \uF{7}{} & \uF{11}{}\tabularnewline
\uF{6}{} & \uF{6}{} & \uT{8}{} & \uT{10}{}\tabularnewline
\end{tabular}}
\end{itemize}
\end{columns}
\begin{block}<12->{}
We say that $p\vee\sim q$ and $q\rightarrow p$ are \emph{equivalent}
\emph{expressions}, written $p\vee\sim q\equiv q\rightarrow p$.
\end{block}
\end{frame}

\begin{frame}{Equivalent expressions}

\begin{block}{Equivalence}
Symbolic expressions that have identical truth values are called
\emph{equivalent expressions}, notated using ``$\equiv$''.
\end{block}
\begin{itemize}
\item [ex.]<2->$p\vee\sim q\equiv p\rightarrow q$
\item [ex.]<3->''It is raining''\\
``It is not the case, that it is not raining''

\begin{itemize}
\item []<4->$q\equiv\sim(\sim q)$
\end{itemize}
\item [ex.]<4->''If the streets are wet then it is raining''\\
``If it is not raining then the streets are not wet.''

\begin{itemize}
\item []<5->$q\rightarrow p\equiv\sim p\rightarrow\sim q$
\end{itemize}
\end{itemize}
\end{frame}

\begin{frame}{Equivalent expressions}

\prob{1}{}{Determine whether the two statements are equivalent.}{\center
\begin{itemize}
\item She is unemployed or she does not have a high school diploma.

\begin{frame}{De Morgan's Law}

\begin{block}{De Morgan's Law}

\begin{itemize}
\item []<2->$\sim(p\wedge q)\equiv\sim p\vee\sim q$
\item []<3->$\sim(p\vee q)\equiv\sim p\wedge\sim q$
\end{itemize}
\end{block}
\ex{4}{}{Negate the following statements
\begin{itemize}
\item []I have a college degree, and I am not employed.
\end{itemize}
}
\begin{columns}


\column{4cm}
\begin{itemize}
\item []<5->$p$: I have a college degree.
\item []<5->$q$: I am not employed.
\end{itemize}

\column{7cm}
\begin{itemize}
\item []<6->Negate, $p\wedge q$.
\item []<7->$\sim(p\wedge q)$
\item []<8->$\equiv\sim p$\_$\sim q$
\item []<9->$\equiv\sim p$$\vee\sim q$
\end{itemize}
\end{columns}
\end{frame}

\begin{frame}{De Morgan's Law}

\begin{block}{Negation}

\begin{itemize}
\item []<2->Negation of \emph{negation}: $\sim(\sim p)\equiv p$
\item []<2->Negation of \emph{conjunction}: $\sim(p\wedge q)\equiv\sim p\vee\sim q$
\item []<3->Negation of \emph{disjunction}: $\sim(p\vee q)\equiv\sim p\wedge\sim q$
\item []<4->Negation of \emph{conditional}: $\sim(p\rightarrow q)\equiv p\wedge\sim q$
\end{itemize}
\end{block}
\vspace{-.5cm}
\begin{columns}


\column{4.5cm}
\begin{itemize}
\item [] \only<5->{%
\begin{tabular}{cc|c|c}
\textbf{$p$} & \textbf{$q$} & $p\rightarrow q$ & \textbf{$\sim p\vee q$}\tabularnewline
\hline 
\uT{5}{} & \uT{5}{} & \uT{6}{} & \uT{10}{}\tabularnewline
\uT{5}{} & \uF{5}{} & \uF{7}{} & \uF{11}{}\tabularnewline
\uF{5}{} & \uT{5}{} & \uT{8}{} & \uT{12}{}\tabularnewline
\uF{5}{} & \uF{5}{} & \uT{9}{} & \uT{13}{}\tabularnewline
\end{tabular}}
\end{itemize}

\column{6.5cm}
\begin{itemize}
\item []<14-> So, $p\rightarrow q\equiv\sim p\vee q$.
\item []<15-> So then $\sim(p\rightarrow q)\equiv\sim(\sim p\vee q)$.
\item []<16-> By De Morgan's Law,
\item []<16->\textrm{ $\sim(\sim p\vee q)\equiv\sim(\sim p)\wedge\sim q\equiv p\wedge\sim q$.}
\item []<17->$\therefore$ $\sim(p\rightarrow q)\equiv p\wedge\sim q$
\end{itemize}
\end{columns}
\end{frame}
